source_metadata.title: Inflammatory Bowel Disease
source_metadata.source_type: clinical review / practice review (secondary source; not a primary study or ACP clinical guideline)

atoms.canonical_statement: The review summarizes evidence-based strategies for screening, prevention, and practice improvement in outpatient health maintenance for adults with inflammatory bowel disease.
The American College of Physicians is listed as the funding source for this In the Clinic article.
The article states that all relevant financial relationships were mitigated and that disclosure forms are available online.
The article states that In the Clinic does not necessarily represent official American College of Physicians clinical policy.
Inflammatory bowel disease comprises Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis and is described as a chronic, relapsing-remitting, immune-mediated gastrointestinal disease with rising global prevalence.
The review reports that an estimated 2.4 million to 3.1 million people in the United States live with inflammatory bowel disease.
The review reports that approximately 80% of patients with inflammatory bowel disease require hospitalization over the disease course.
The review reports that approximately 50% of patients with Crohn disease require bowel surgery.
The review reports that approximately 20% of patients with ulcerative colitis require bowel surgery.
Contemporary inflammatory bowel disease management uses a treat-to-target strategy with periodic biomarkers and endoscopic assessment rather than symptom control alone.
Early effective therapy, particularly biologic therapy in Crohn disease, is favored to achieve deep remission before irreversible bowel damage occurs.
Systemic corticosteroids should not be used as long-term maintenance therapy for inflammatory bowel disease.
High-quality inflammatory bowel disease care requires coordinated responsibility among gastroenterology, primary care, and patients for preventive care, monitoring, and comorbidity management.

source_anchor.paragraph: General approach to health care maintenance

atoms.canonical_statement: Routine attention to depression, anxiety, fatigue, and financial strain is recommended as part of longitudinal inflammatory bowel disease care.
In a Scandinavian cohort of 96,447 patients with ulcerative colitis, colorectal cancer incidence was 1.29 per 1000 person-years with a hazard ratio of 1.66 versus the background population.

quantitative_result.effect_measure: hazard ratio for colorectal cancer incidence

atoms.canonical_statement: In the same ulcerative colitis cohort, colorectal cancer mortality was 0.55 per 1000 person-years with a hazard ratio of 1.59 versus the background population.

quantitative_result.effect_measure: hazard ratio for colorectal cancer mortality

atoms.canonical_statement: In a Scandinavian cohort of 47,035 patients with Crohn disease, colorectal cancer incidence was 0.82 per 1000 person-years with a hazard ratio of 1.40 versus the background population.

quantitative_result.effect_measure: hazard ratio for colorectal cancer incidence

atoms.canonical_statement: In the same Crohn disease cohort, colorectal cancer mortality was 0.47 per 1000 person-years with a hazard ratio of 1.74 versus the background population.

quantitative_result.effect_measure: hazard ratio for colorectal cancer mortality

atoms.canonical_statement: Among patients with Crohn disease who developed colorectal cancer, stage-adjusted risk of colorectal cancer death remained higher than in the background population, with a hazard ratio of 1.42.

population.label: Patients with Crohn disease who developed colorectal cancer

atoms.canonical_statement: Initial colorectal cancer surveillance colonoscopy is recommended 8 to 10 years after symptom onset for patients with inflammatory bowel disease involving the colon.
For patients with primary sclerosing cholangitis and inflammatory bowel disease, surveillance colonoscopy is recommended at inflammatory bowel disease diagnosis and annually thereafter.

U.S. guidance summarized in the review supports annual colorectal surveillance for higher-risk colonic inflammatory bowel disease and extension to every 2 to 3 years in lower-risk patients after consecutive negative examinations.

Patients with inflammatory bowel disease receiving thiopurines, biologic agents, or targeted small molecules should generally undergo annual total-body skin examination; surveillance should continue after thiopurine discontinuation.

Cervical cancer screening in women with inflammatory bowel disease should follow age-appropriate USPSTF recommendations, with some guidance supporting shorter intervals during immunosuppressive therapy.
The review reports that perianal Crohn disease was associated with higher anorectal cancer risk than nonperianal Crohn disease, with an odds ratio of 4.67.

population.label: Patients with inflammatory bowel disease in the epiIIRN cohort

atoms.canonical_statement: DEXA screening is recommended for patients with inflammatory bowel disease who have risk factors such as BMI below 20 kg/m², cumulative systemic corticosteroid exposure above 3 months at prednisone-equivalent at least 7.5 mg/day or repeated courses, smoking, postmenopausal status, or hypogonadism.

Patients with inflammatory bowel disease should receive annual malnutrition screening and annual vitamin D, ferritin, and transferrin saturation testing; vitamin B12 should be checked annually in patients with ileal disease or ileal resection.
For iron deficiency monitoring, the review suggests testing about every 6 to 12 months in remission or mild disease and about every 3 months during active disease.
Latent tuberculosis screening is recommended before initiation of most immunosuppressive therapies for inflammatory bowel disease, particularly TNF antagonists and JAK inhibitors.
A meta-analysis summarized in the review found 45 tuberculosis cases among 7,912 TNF-antagonist recipients versus 3 among 3,967 controls, corresponding to an odds ratio of 1.94.
Universal hepatitis B screening with HBsAg, anti-HBs, and anti-HBc is recommended before immunosuppressive therapy in patients with inflammatory bowel disease.

Patients who are HBsAg-positive and receive moderate- to high-dose corticosteroids or other immunosuppressive therapy for more than 4 weeks are described as high risk for HBV reactivation, with antiviral prophylaxis strongly recommended rather than monitoring alone.
Across 12 randomized trials summarized in the review, antiviral prophylaxis was associated with an 82% relative reduction in HBV reactivation compared with monitoring alone.

population.label: HBsAg-positive and/or anti-HBc-positive patients in 12 randomized trials

atoms.canonical_statement: Across the same 12 randomized trials, antiviral prophylaxis was associated with a 72% relative reduction in hepatitis flare related to HBV reactivation.

population.label: HBsAg-positive and/or anti-HBc-positive patients in 12 randomized trials

concept.text: Hepatitis flare related to HBV reactivation

atoms.canonical_statement: USPSTF one-time universal hepatitis C screening in adults aged 18 years or older and screening during pregnancy apply to patients with inflammatory bowel disease.
Routine USPSTF HIV screening applies to patients with inflammatory bowel disease, and some professional societies additionally recommend HIV testing before immunosuppressive therapy.

Before immunosuppressive therapy, varicella immunity should be assessed from reliable infection history or documentation of a 2-dose varicella vaccine series; routine serology is not recommended in previously vaccinated people.

MMR immunity should be assessed by documentation of a 2-dose vaccination series before immunosuppressive therapy; routine MMR serology is not recommended because commercial assays have limited sensitivity.
A systematic review summarized in the article found pooled prevalence of depression symptoms of 25% among adults with inflammatory bowel disease.

population.label: Adults with inflammatory bowel disease across 75 studies

atoms.canonical_statement: A systematic review summarized in the article found pooled prevalence of anxiety symptoms of 32% among adults with inflammatory bowel disease.

population.label: Adults with inflammatory bowel disease across 58 studies

atoms.canonical_statement: Annual screening for depression and anxiety is recommended for all adults with inflammatory bowel disease, using standard primary-care tools such as PHQ-2/PHQ-9 and GAD-7 when appropriate.
Women with inflammatory bowel disease planning pregnancy should receive preconception counseling and aim for clinical remission for at least 3 to 6 months before conception.

Methotrexate, JAK inhibitors, and sphingosine-1-phosphate receptor modulators are described as contraindicated during pregnancy and breastfeeding and should be discontinued at least 3 months before conception.

source_anchor.paragraph: Safety of IBD medication during pregnancy

atoms.canonical_statement: The review recommends continuation of biologics, thiopurines, and 5-aminosalicylates during pregnancy when needed to maintain inflammatory bowel disease remission.

source_anchor.paragraph: Safety of IBD medication during pregnancy

atoms.canonical_statement: For vaccine guidance in this review, immunosuppressive therapy includes systemic corticosteroids at prednisone-equivalent at least 20 mg/day or any dose for at least 14 days, thiopurines, methotrexate, biologics, JAK inhibitors, and sphingosine-1-phosphate receptor modulators.

Recombinant zoster vaccine is recommended for patients with inflammatory bowel disease receiving or expected to receive immunosuppressive therapy from age 19 years, and for all adults with inflammatory bowel disease aged 50 years or older regardless of therapy.

PCV20 or PCV21 is presented as the preferred single-vaccine pneumococcal strategy for vaccine-naive patients with inflammatory bowel disease aged 50 years or older and for patients aged 19 to 49 years receiving immunosuppressive therapy.
Annual inactivated influenza vaccination is recommended for all adults with inflammatory bowel disease; live attenuated intranasal influenza vaccine should be avoided during immunosuppression.
HPV vaccination should follow CDC/ACIP guidance, with a 3-dose series for immunocompromised patients and shared decision making for previously unvaccinated adults aged 27 to 45 years.
Patients with inflammatory bowel disease should follow ACIP COVID-19 vaccination recommendations; COVID-19 vaccines are nonlive and may be given during immunosuppressive therapy.
Hepatitis A vaccination is recommended for patients with inflammatory bowel disease, and hepatitis B vaccination is recommended for those without prior immunity.

After a completed hepatitis B vaccine series with anti-HBs below 10 mIU/mL, the review describes a single challenge dose followed by anti-HBs testing 4 to 8 weeks later; failure to reach at least 10 mIU/mL should prompt a repeated vaccine series.

RSV vaccination is recommended for all adults with inflammatory bowel disease aged at least 75 years and for adults aged 50 to 74 years with chronic conditions or other risk factors for severe RSV infection, including immunosuppressive therapy.
MMR vaccine should be given only when a patient with inflammatory bowel disease is not immunosuppressed and immunosuppressive therapy is not anticipated within the next 4 weeks.
Patients with inflammatory bowel disease should use sun-protective behaviors, and those receiving immunosuppressive therapy should have annual total-body skin examination.
Bone health maintenance should include total calcium intake of about 1000 to 1200 mg/day and vitamin D supplementation sufficient to maintain 25-hydroxyvitamin D at least 30 ng/mL.
Regular weight-bearing aerobic activity and progressive resistance training 2 to 3 times per week are recommended to support bone health in patients with inflammatory bowel disease.

Intravenous iron is recommended as first-line therapy for iron deficiency in patients with inflammatory bowel disease when hemoglobin is below 10 g/dL; oral iron is reasonable for mild anemia or inactive disease.
For documented vitamin B12 deficiency, the review favors parenteral replacement, typically 1000 μg intramuscularly or subcutaneously every 1 to 4 weeks on a long-term basis.
The review states that cardiovascular risk is about 2- to 3-fold higher during active inflammatory bowel disease than during remission.

Long-term immunosuppressive therapy generally warrants complete blood count, liver chemistries, and serum creatinine every 3 to 6 months, with more frequent monitoring during the first 3 to 6 months after initiation or dose escalation.
Patients receiving 5-aminosalicylates should have periodic renal function testing and urinalysis, while patients receiving JAK inhibitors should have baseline and follow-up lipid panels.
All patients with inflammatory bowel disease who smoke should receive structured smoking cessation counseling and support.
Health maintenance quality indicators include documenting immunization status and timely administration of indicated vaccines.
Health maintenance quality indicators include adherence to colorectal cancer surveillance intervals in patients with colonic inflammatory bowel disease.
Health maintenance quality indicators include latent tuberculosis and hepatitis B screening before advanced immunosuppressive therapy, especially TNF antagonists and JAK inhibitors.
Health maintenance quality indicators include thiopurine methyltransferase genotype or enzyme activity testing before thiopurine therapy.
Health maintenance quality indicators include timely transition from corticosteroids to corticosteroid-sparing therapy.
Health maintenance quality indicators include testing for Clostridioides difficile in patients presenting with acute inflammatory bowel disease flares regardless of recent antibiotic exposure.
The review identifies AGA, ACG, and ECCO guidance as key sources for evidence-based inflammatory bowel disease health maintenance recommendations.

extraction_limitations: This source is a secondary clinical review/practice review, not a primary study; the LiteratureAtom MVP is optimized for primary literature.

Quantitative findings attributed to cited cohorts/meta-analyses are retained as review-level secondary reports and tagged secondary_reported_result; they are not represented as results generated by this article.
Practice recommendations are review-level syntheses and are tagged review_recommendation rather than treated as guideline recommendations generated by the article.
Supplement Figure 1 and Supplement Table 1 are referenced by the article but were not supplied as companion materials and were not used for extraction.
